title: How can paper cutouts test for four angles of symmetry?
description: The four-arm figure is drawn twice, and the arms of one copy are cut out. The cutout is pinned at the centre and turned over the fixed figure, and each exact fit is noted. Keeko's doubt is that sliding the cutout checks a turn too.
teaching_notes: One idea: pin the cutout at the centre and turn it, because a turn keeps the centre still. Watch for students who slide the cutout over the figure instead of turning it.

source: To check if a figure with radial arms has 4 angles of symmet
video_script.why: The child learns to test a radial-arm figure for rotational symmetry by turning a pinned paper cutout over the fixed figure.
video_script.substitution: the book's paper cutout of the arms, turned over the same figure drawn on a second paper
video_script.anchor: the book's four-arm figure drawn on two pieces of paper
video_script.wrong_answer: slide the cutout over the figure
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko slides the cutout across the figure without a pin and calls it a check.
video_script.payoff_line: The cutout fits only at four turns

final_answer.value: The cutout fits exactly at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° only
final_answer.spoken: the cutout fits exactly at ninety, one hundred eighty, two hundred seventy and three hundred sixty degrees only

maths_rules: draw the figure twice; cut the arms out of one copy; keep the other copy fixed
pin the cutout at the centre so that the centre stays still, then turn it
the cutout fits the fixed figure after 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°
between these turns the arms do not sit on arms, so there are 4 angles of symmetry
sliding without a pin is not a turn, so it checks nothing
video_script.design: Two copies of the four-arm figure. A teal cutout is pinned on top of the fixed copy and turned. A tick counter fills at each exact fit. Keeko's doubt is that sliding also checks.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, about checking a figure.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The four-arm figure is drawn on two pieces of paper.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How can paper cutouts show how many angles of symmetry it has?

beats.on_screen: the two papers stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the left paper with the figure fixed; the right paper with the arms cut out; the words angle of symmetry beside a curved arrow

marks.fixed: the left paper stays fixed on the board
marks.cut: the arms are cut out of the right paper
marks.name: the words angle of symmetry appear beside a curved arrow

narration: <bookmark mark='fixed'/>One paper stays fixed on the table.
<bookmark mark='cut'/>From the other paper, we cut out the radial arms.
<bookmark mark='name'/>A turn after which the figure looks the same is called an angle of symmetry.
The cutout will show us these turns.

beats.on_screen: Given: the figure with 4 radial arms drawn on two papers; the arms are cut out of one paper
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the four-arm figure is drawn on two papers.
The arms are cut out of one paper.

beats.on_screen: To find: the turns after which the cutout fits the fixed figure
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the turns after which the cutout fits the figure.

beats.on_screen: put the cutout on the fixed figure and pin it through the centre

marks.pin: the cutout is laid on the fixed figure and a pin goes through the centre

narration: <bookmark mark='pin'/>Step one, lay the cutout exactly on the fixed figure.
Push a pin through the centre, so the centre cannot move.

beats.on_screen: turn the cutout slowly; a tick appears each time its arms sit exactly on the arms: 90°, then 180°, then 270°, then 360°

marks.turn: the cutout turns slowly about the pin
marks.tick: a tick appears at each exact fit, with the turn written beside it
marks.more: the last two ticks appear, at 270° and 360°

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Step two, turn the cutout slowly about the pin.
<bookmark mark='tick'/>It fits after ninety degrees, then after one hundred eighty degrees.
<bookmark mark='more'/>It fits again after two hundred seventy degrees, and after a full turn of three hundred sixty degrees.

beats.on_screen: between the ticks the arms of the cutout fall between the arms of the figure: there is no fit

marks.between: the cutout is held at a turn between two ticks and its arms fall between the arms

narration: <bookmark mark='between'/>Step three, look between the fits.
At any other turn, the arms of the cutout fall between the arms of the figure.
There is no fit there.

beats.on_screen: Answer: The cutout fits exactly at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° only
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The cutout fits only at four turns.
They are ninety, one hundred eighty, two hundred seventy and three hundred sixty degrees.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the two papers
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble from Keeko says slide it; the cutout slides across the figure and no pin is shown; the bubble is struck out and the pin returns

marks.slide: the cutout slides across the figure
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and the pin returns to the centre

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we can slide the cutout over the figure.
<bookmark mark='slide'/>Slide it, and the arms may land on arms, but nothing has turned.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>A turn needs the centre to stay still, so the pin must stay.
